newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil co-op looks at producing organic coffee.
newsitem.headline: Brazil co-op looks at producing organic coffee.

text.p: A Brazilian coffee cooperative has embarked on a study which could result in the production of organic coffee in five years' time, a cooperative official said.

The Sao Sebastiao do Paraiso cooperative in Minas Gerais began a program in December with Brazil's Agricultural Research Company, Embrapa, to find natural ways to fight problems such as the broca beetle and fungi such as leaf rust.
"In the next five years we could be in a situation to say some coffee is totally organic," said Rogerio Araujo, technical director at the cooperative.
The attraction for growers is reduced costs and higher revenues from a growing niche in the international market.
"Today fertilizers, pesticides and other inputs represent around 47 percent of the cost of production," Araujo said.
"At the same time there is a niche in the international market for organic coffee which can have up to 20 percent better returns, particularly in the Japanese market," he added.
At present Embrapa is monitoring production in an area of half an hectare containing 3,300 trees.
"But this could be increased at any stage as there are already other people interested," said Embrapa's Marta Ricci who is working on the project.
The fear is of moving too quickly and suddenly stopping the use of all chemicals which is why it is expected to take several years before coffee is grown completely free of chemicals.
"Things can't be changed overnight. Coffee is these people's bread and butter so we have to be sure that we have ruled out all the risks," Ricci said.
Moreover coffee can also only be called organic if it has been one whole crop year without chemicals, Araujo said.
Normal coffee production in the area is around one million bags and at this stage it is difficult to say what percentage of this could become organically grown coffee, he added.
A few individual growers have been producing organic coffee in Brazil but officials say this is the first time a major cooperative has embarked on such a project.
"I think it is highly commendable that Sao Sebastiao should be looking at it," said Luis Hafers, president of the Brazilian Rural Society.
"I basically think that the buyer is always right and if the buyer wants it, we should be producing it. Also we should learn a lot of lessons from their project," he added.
The higher revenue, lower costs of organic coffee has already attracted growers in other Latin American countries such as Nicaragua and Mexico.
